problem: Source: 'for some error of pronunciation, or some inattention to stops' — 'stops' means punctuation (pauses when reading aloud). MODERN 'some lapse in attention' loses what she was inattentive to and makes it a general distraction.
new_text: During the course of the day I was enrolled in the fourth class and given regular lessons and tasks. Until now I had only been a spectator at Lowood; I was about to become a participant. At first, being unaccustomed to learning things by heart, the lessons seemed both long and difficult. The constant switching from one subject to another bewildered me, and I was glad when, around three in the afternoon, Miss Smith put a two-yard strip of muslin into my hands along with a needle and thimble and sent me to sit in a quiet corner of the schoolroom to hem it. At that hour most of the others were sewing too. But one class still stood around Miss Scatcherd's chair, reading aloud. Since everything was quiet, I could hear the subject of their lesson and how each girl performed, along with Miss Scatcherd's criticisms or occasional praise. It was English history. Among the readers I noticed my new acquaintance from the garden. At the start of the lesson, she'd been at the top of the class, but for some error of pronunciation or some inattention to punctuation, she was suddenly sent to the very bottom. problem: Source ends 'the inside was further beyond his interference than he imagined.' MODERN 'the inside was far beyond his reach' drops 'than he imagined', losing the irony about Brocklehurst's self-deception.
new_text: Miss Temple passed her handkerchief across her lips, as if smoothing away an involuntary smile. She gave the order, though, and when the first class understood what was being asked, they obeyed. Leaning back on my bench a little, I could see the looks and grimaces they exchanged. It was a pity Mr. Brocklehurst couldn't see them too—he might have realized that however much he controlled the outside of the cup and platter, the inside was further beyond his reach than he imagined.

problem: Source: 'treated as an equal by those of my own age, and not molested by any' — i.e. nobody bullied her. MODERN 'and left alone by everyone else' reads as being ignored/excluded, reversing the positive sense.
new_text: Before the half hour was up, five o'clock struck. School was dismissed and everyone went to the dining hall for tea. I dared to climb down from the stool. It was deep dusk. I retreated to a corner and sat on the floor. The spell that had sustained me began to dissolve. Reaction set in, and soon the grief that seized me was so overwhelming that I collapsed face-down on the floor. Now I cried. Helen Burns wasn't there. Nothing held me up. Left to myself, I gave in completely, and my tears soaked the floorboards. I had meant to be so good, and to do so much at Lowood—to make friends, earn respect, and win affection. That very morning I had already made real progress: I'd reached the head of my class. Miss Miller had praised me warmly. Miss Temple had smiled with approval and promised to teach me drawing and let me start French if I kept improving for another two months. I had been welcomed by my fellow students—treated as an equal by those my age, and bullied by no one. And now here I was, crushed and trampled again. Would I ever be able to rise?

problem: Source: Miss Temple's serenity, stately mien and refined language 'precluded deviation into the ardent, the excited, the eager' — describing her own manner. MODERN 'kept any conversation from becoming too heated or emotional' shifts the restraint onto the conversation in general; 'of state in her mien' is also folded away.
new_text: Miss Temple always had something serene in her air, stately in her bearing, and refined and proper in her speech, which kept her from ever straying into anything ardent, excited, or eager. There was something about her that tempered the pleasure of watching and listening with a restraining sense of awe—and that was what I felt now. But as for Helen Burns, I was struck with amazement.
